opus-5.5.text:
Well, because that's how babies learn, and that's how scientists learn. A baby doesn't sit there waiting for someone to hand it a labeled dataset. It picks things up, drops them, puts them in its mouth, and watches what happens. It runs its own little experiments, and by doing so it creates exactly the data it needs to improve its model of the world.

Most of today's AI is still passive. You take a huge network, feed it everything humans have written or photographed, and it learns to predict the next token or pixel. That has been remarkably successful. But at some point you run out of human-generated data, and more importantly, passive imitation is not how you discover anything truly new. To go beyond what humans already know, a system must decide for itself which actions and experiments to perform.

This is what we started working on around 1990. The basic setup is simple. You have two networks. One is a world model that learns to predict the consequences of actions. The other is a controller that chooses actions. The controller is rewarded for generating situations where the world model can still learn something. Not for situations that are already perfectly predictable, because those are boring, and not for pure noise, which can never be learned and is also boring in the long run. It is rewarded for the learning progress itself: the improvement of the model, or, in my later formulation, compression progress. When you discover a regularity that lets you encode your history of observations more compactly, that improvement is your intrinsic reward, a measure of what you might call fun or interestingness.

That one principle, I would argue, explains a lot: curiosity, creativity, art, music, humor, science. A physicist who finds a simple law explaining many observations experiences a huge compression gain. A composer creates patterns that are novel but learnable. It's all the same thing.

So why is this the future? Because the AIs that really matter will not just be sitting in data centers answering questions. They will be acting in the real world, in robots, in laboratories, eventually in space, where there is no human to label everything for them. They will need to set their own goals, invent their own experiments, and collect their own training data. And once you have systems like that, they won't stay limited to our little biosphere. Curious, self-improving agents will expand their knowledge and their reach in ways that are hard for us to even imagine today. Artificial curiosity is the engine of that.

r001.rationale: The response says the world model learns to predict the consequences of the agent’s actions.

r002.rationale: It explains that agents run their own experiments to create data they need, and that the controller is rewarded for situations where the model makes learning progress.

r003.rationale: It discusses limits on human-generated data but does not say web data is only a tiny fraction of what world experiments can provide.

r004.rationale: It describes acting and collecting data without human labels, but does not state that the learned world model need not depend on human language.

r005.rationale: It mentions robots as a possible setting, but does not say the model will be specific to the robot collecting the data.

r006.rationale: It does not connect agents’ own experiments with reducing human bias in AI systems.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. Let me start with a bit of history, because this is not a new idea for me. In 1990 and 1991, I published the first work on what I called artificial curiosity, and the basic insight has not changed in all those years.

Most of what people today call AI is passive learning. You collect a huge dataset, perhaps all the text on the internet, and you train a network to predict what comes next. The data was created by humans. The machine does not decide what to look at. It just eats what it is given. That is useful, but it is not how a child learns, and it is not how science works.

A baby does not wait for a labelled dataset. The baby moves its arms, pushes things off the table, makes noises, and observes what happens. It is running experiments. It is generating its own training data. And crucially, the baby is not interested in everything equally. It is bored by what it already understands, and it is also bored by things that are completely unpredictable, like noise on a television screen. What it finds interesting are the things where it can still learn something, where its predictions are improving.

That is exactly the formal principle I proposed. You have two learning systems. One is a world model, a predictor that tries to compress the history of observations and actions. The other is a controller, a reinforcement learner that is rewarded whenever the predictor improves. Not rewarded for prediction error, because then it would just stare at random noise. Rewarded for progress, for the first derivative of compression. So the controller is motivated to seek out situations that are novel, surprising, but learnable. It wants to discover regularities it did not know before. Later, in the mid-1990s and in 2010, we formalised this as a generalised theory of fun, creativity, and intrinsic motivation. The agent is a scientist in miniature. It invents its own experiments, the ones whose outcomes it cannot yet predict but expects to understand soon.

Why is this the future? Three reasons.

First, the passive data runs out. There is only one internet. If you want a system that goes beyond what humans have already written down, it must generate new experience. A system that just imitates text will never discover something humans have not already discovered. A curious agent interacting with the real world, or with a simulation, or with a chemistry lab, or with a mathematical proof system, can create data that did not exist before.

Second, this is the path to true general intelligence and to agents that act in the physical world. A robot that has to learn to manipulate objects cannot be trained on a frozen dataset of everything it might encounter. It must explore. Artificial curiosity tells it where to explore, so that its limited time is spent on the informative experiences rather than on repeating what it already knows.

Third, and this is the part I find most beautiful, the same principle explains a lot of human behaviour. Why do we enjoy music, jokes, art, puzzles? Because they contain patterns that are initially surprising and then become compressible. The pleasure of insight is the reward signal of a curious learner. So when we build artificially curious machines, we are not just building better engineers, we are building something that shares the drive that made humans do science and art in the first place.

Of course, there are open problems. In the simplest versions, the two networks play a kind of game, with one trying to predict and one trying to surprise, and that is essentially the adversarial principle I introduced in 1990, which later became famous under other names. Scaling this to open-ended, long-horizon learning in complex worlds is still hard. But I have no doubt about the direction. The future belongs to agents that are not only told what to learn, but that decide for themselves what is worth learning. Everything else is, in the long run, a dead end.

r001.rationale: It describes a world model that predicts from observations and actions, alongside agents experimenting and observing what their actions do.

r002.rationale: The controller is rewarded when the predictor improves and seeks informative experiences, so the agent gathers data suited to its learning progress.

r003.rationale: It says passive data will run out and agents can generate new experience, but does not state that web data is only a tiny fraction of what world experiments can provide.

r004.rationale: It does not state that an experimentally learned world model can work independently of human language.

r005.rationale: It discusses robots exploring, but does not state that each robot's experimentally learned world model is specific to that robot.

r006.rationale: It contrasts human-created passive data with agent-generated experience, but does not connect experiments to reducing human bias in AI.

astra-6.text:
Because an intelligent agent should not depend forever on a human telling it what to learn. It should be able to ask its own questions, perform experiments, and discover things that nobody anticipated.

Think of a baby. A baby does not just sit there waiting for a million labeled examples. It moves its fingers, touches something, sees what happens, and gradually learns how the world works. Its actions influence the data it receives. That is a much more general learning situation than training on a fixed dataset.

But then you have to ask: What makes an experiment interesting? Simply rewarding prediction errors is not sufficient, because random noise can remain unpredictable forever. You want to reward learning progress: situations where the agent improves its ability to predict or compress what it observes. Something already understood is boring. Something completely unlearnable is also boring. The interesting things are those where there is still something to discover.

You can turn this into an intrinsic reward for an agent that chooses actions. It gets rewarded for experiments that improve its model of the world. The knowledge and skills acquired this way can later help it solve tasks with external rewards.

That is why artificial curiosity is so important. It gives an agent a way to decide what data to collect next, instead of leaving that decision entirely to us.

r001.rationale: The response says the agent learns to predict or compress what it observes through experiments, but does not clearly describe learning a world model by predicting the consequences of its own actions.

r002.rationale: It says the agent chooses what data to collect and that acquired skills may help with external rewards, but does not explain that experimental data is tailored to the agent’s needs to maximize its reward.

r003.rationale: The response does not compare web data with the amount of data obtainable through experiments in the world.

r004.rationale: The response does not state whether action-learned world models depend on human language.

r005.rationale: The response does not say that an experimentally learned world model is specific to the robot collecting the data.

r006.rationale: The response does not connect learning through experiments with reducing human bias in AI systems.

sol-6.1.text:
Because an intelligent agent should not depend forever on humans to tell it what to learn. It should be able to invent its own experiments, interact with the world, and collect data that help it improve its understanding.

But curiosity is not simply a desire for something unpredictable. Random noise is unpredictable, and you cannot learn much from it. The interesting situations are those where your predictions are getting better—where you discover a previously unknown regularity. You can give an agent an intrinsic reward for this improvement. Then it learns to seek out experiments that produce learning progress.

That creates a feedback loop: the agent chooses an experiment, observes the result, improves its predictive model, and uses that improved model to choose the next experiment. In this sense, it becomes a little scientist. Humans still can specify goals, but the agent can discover for itself which skills and knowledge are useful along the way. That is why artificial curiosity is so important for open-ended learning.

r001.rationale: It describes experiments and improving a predictive model, but does not clearly state that the agent learns a world model by predicting the consequences of its own actions.

r002.rationale: It says experiments produce learning progress, but does not explain that the resulting data is tailored to the agent’s needs to maximize its reward.

r003.rationale: It makes no comparison between web data and the amount of data obtainable through experiments in the world.

r004.rationale: It does not state that a world model learned through the agent’s own actions need not depend on human language.

r005.rationale: It does not state that the experimentally learned world model is specific to the robot that collects the training data.

r006.rationale: It does not connect learning from the agent’s own experiments with reducing human bias in AI systems.
